sections.h: Healing at Bethesda: "My Father is at work"
sections.b: In John 5 Jesus heals a man on a Sabbath and tells him to carry his mat, which the Temple authorities count as forbidden work (Jeremiah 17:21–22; Nehemiah 13:19). Jesus's defense is not about the rules but about God: "My Father is at work right up to now, and I am at work too" (John 5:17). Jewish teachers asked the same question, how God can rest while the world goes on; Philo said God never stops making, and later rabbis said God works on the Sabbath only by giving life and judging (Genesis Rabbah 11:10). Jesus claims those very works (John 5:21–22), which is why his hearers say he makes himself equal to God (John 5:18).

common: Jesus healed on the Sabbath on purpose, to show what the day is for.
uncommon: Some scholars read John 5:17 as a claim that the true Sabbath rest of God has not yet come, so God's work continues until the new creation.

sections.h: The pool of Bethesda
sections.b: John 5 is set at a pool near the Sheep Gate where the sick gathered, believing the first one into the stirred water would be cured; later manuscripts add an angel to explain it (John 5:4). Excavations near St. Anne's Church found a double pool (how its porches stood is debated), and the site later held a shrine of the healing god Asclepius. Jesus heals a man ill for thirty-eight years with a word, without the water and without the man's faith, and warns him about sin while elsewhere denying that suffering always comes from sin (John 5:14; John 9:2–3).

sections.h: The true bread from heaven
sections.b: In John 6 the crowd quotes "Bread from heaven he gave them to eat" (John 6:31) and asks for a sign like Moses' manna. Some Jews hoped the Messiah would bring the manna back (2 Baruch 29:8; Ecclesiastes Rabbah 1:9). Jesus corrects the giver (not Moses but the Father), the tense (the Father "gives" now), and the bread itself: "I am the bread of life" (John 6:35). The manna fed for a day and the fathers died; this bread gives eternal life (John 6:49–51). Peder Borgen argued that John 6:31–58 is built like a Jewish sermon on the manna text.

common: The manna is a picture of Jesus, the bread from heaven.

sections.h: Eating his flesh and drinking his blood (John 6)
sections.b: John tells no institution of the Supper at the Last Supper, but John 6 speaks of eating Jesus's flesh and drinking his blood (John 6:51–58), after a Passover-time meal where Jesus "gave thanks" (John 6:11, 23). Catholic and Orthodox Christians read it as teaching the Eucharist; Luther and Calvin read it as feeding on Christ by faith, which the Supper seals; Zwingli used John 6:63, "the flesh is of no use," against a bodily presence. Many modern scholars hear both: faith in the crucified Jesus, and the church's meal.

common: John 6 is the Bible's fullest teaching on what Communion means.
uncommon: Some scholars think John 6:51–58 was added to the discourse in a later edition of the Gospel to bring in the Eucharist.

sections.h: "Unless the Father draws him"
sections.b: John 6 sets God's action beside human coming: everything the Father gives will come to Jesus (John 6:37), no one can come unless the Father draws him (John 6:44), and coming is the Father's gift (John 6:65). Yet whoever comes will never be thrown out, and the hearers are blamed for not believing (John 6:36–37, 64). Augustine said the Father draws by delight, not force. Calvinist readers see an effective drawing of the elect; Arminian, Wesleyan, Catholic and Orthodox readers join it to John 12:32, a drawing of all that can be refused.

sections.h: Those the Father gives the Son
sections.b: John speaks of believers as a gift from the Father to the Son, in the neuter: "Everything the Father gives me" (John 6:37; compare John 6:39; compare John 17:2, 24). Jesus promises to lose none of it and to raise it up on the last day. Readers who stress election see a fixed people; others note that the same verse invites "anyone who comes" and that Jesus chose the Twelve, one of whom was "a devil" (John 6:70).

sections.h: "Equal to God": the Son who does the Father's work
sections.b: In John 5 the authorities charge Jesus with making himself equal to God (John 5:18). His answer both affirms and qualifies: the Son does nothing on his own, only what he sees the Father doing (John 5:19), yet the Father gives him the works that belong to God alone, giving life and judging, so that all may honor the Son as they honor the Father (John 5:21–23). The fathers of the church used the passage against Arius: equal in honor, receiving all from the Father. Unitarians and Jehovah's Witnesses read "equal to God" as the opponents' charge, which Jesus answers by saying he does nothing on his own (John 5:19).

sections.h: Judge because he is the Son of Man
sections.b: John 5:27 is the only place in the Gospels where the title lacks the article in Greek, exactly as in Daniel 7:13: the Father gives judgment to the one like a son of man. Some read it also as "because he is human." In John 6 the Son of Man gives the food that lasts (John 6:27), gives his flesh and blood (John 6:53), and will be seen going up where he was before (John 6:62).

sections.h: "Moses wrote about me"
sections.b: Jesus tells his accusers that Moses wrote about him (John 5:46), and after the feeding the crowd says, "This man truly is the Prophet, the one coming into the world!" (John 6:14), the prophet Moses promised (Deuteronomy 18:15). They then want to make him king, and Jesus withdraws (John 6:15). John agrees that Jesus is the Prophet but shows him to be more: not a new Moses who gives bread, but the bread God gives.

sections.h: Moses as accuser
sections.b: Jewish tradition remembered Moses as Israel's intercessor (Exodus 32:11–14; Testament of Moses 12:6). In John 5:45–47 Jesus says Moses will be the accuser of those who trust him but reject the one he wrote about. In John 6 the crowd compares Jesus with Moses and the manna, and Jesus answers that it was not Moses who gave the bread from heaven (John 6:32).

sections.h: The second Passover in John
sections.b: John names three Passovers (John 2:13; 6:4; 11:55). The one in John 6 frames the chapter as a new exodus: a meal in the wilderness, a crossing of the sea, bread from heaven, complaining, and finally the words about flesh and blood that point to Jesus's death as the Passover Lamb (John 19:36).

sections.h: Life now and the last day
sections.b: John 5 holds together life already given and a future resurrection. Whoever believes "has eternal life" and "has already moved out of death and into life" (John 5:24); yet an hour is coming when everyone in the tombs will hear the Son's voice and come out, to a resurrection of life or of judgment, echoing Daniel 12:2 (John 5:28–29). In John 6 Jesus promises four times to raise believers up on the last day (John 6:39, 40, 44, 54).

sections.h: "I am" on the sea and "I am the bread of life"
sections.b: John 6 has both kinds of "I am." On the stormy sea Jesus says simply, "I am. Stop being afraid" (John 6:20): it can mean "It's me," but on the waters where only God walks (Job 9:8) it also echoes God's name in Exodus 3:14 and Isaiah 43:10. Then comes the first "I am" with a picture: "I am the bread of life" (John 6:35; 6:48, 51). Like Wisdom in Proverbs 9:5, Jesus offers his bread, but whoever comes to him will not go hungry at all.
sections.refs: John 6:20; John 6:35; John 6:48; John 6:51; Exodus 3:14; Proverbs 9:5

sections.h: Authorities in Jerusalem, a crowd in Galilee (John 5–6)
sections.b: In John 5 "the Jews" are clearly the Temple authorities: the healed man, himself a Jew, reports to them (John 5:15), and they pursue Jesus for Sabbath-breaking and blasphemy (John 5:16–18). In John 6 the same word is used of a crowd in the synagogue at Capernaum who know Jesus's family (John 6:41–42, 52, 59). In chapter 6 it is hard to read the word as only "Judeans" or only "the leaders"; many read it as Jews who resist Jesus wherever they are. Others, such as Steve Mason and Philip Esler, translate it "Judeans" throughout, and some take the Capernaum opponents as Judeans present in Galilee or as John's label for opponents. Their "complaining" echoes Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 16:2).

sections.h: Bethesda by the Sheep Gate
sections.b: John names a pool in Jerusalem beside the Sheep Gate with five porches (John 5:2). The Sheep Gate stood north of the Temple (Nehemiah 3:1). Excavations at St. Anne's Church found a double pool divided by a dam. Most scholars reconstruct porticoes on four sides and across the middle, though some dispute the middle one; the find supports John's knowledge of the city before its destruction in AD 70.

sections.h: Bread in the wilderness again
sections.b: John 6 replays the wilderness: Philip's question echoes Moses' "Where am I to get meat to give this whole people?" (Numbers 11:13), the crowd asks for manna, and the hearers complain as Israel did (Exodus 16:2). The fathers who ate manna in the desert died; whoever eats the bread from heaven will live forever (John 6:49–51).
sections.refs: John 6:5–13; John 6:31; John 6:41; John 6:49–51; Numbers 11:13; Exodus 16:2

sections.h: Barley loaves for a crowd
sections.b: Only John says the five loaves were barley (John 6:9), recalling Elisha, who fed a hundred men with twenty barley loaves and had some left over (2 Kings 4:42–44). In John the bread is less, the crowd far larger, and twelve baskets are left: one greater than Elisha is here.

sections.h: The lake and its towns in John 6
sections.b: John calls the lake both the Sea of Galilee and the Sea of Tiberias (John 6:1; 21:1), after the city Herod Antipas founded about AD 20 and named for the emperor. The feeding happens on the hills across the lake; boats come from Tiberias; and the discourse is spoken in the synagogue at Capernaum (John 6:23–24, 59).

sections.h: "The work of God" is to believe
sections.b: Asked what works God requires, Jesus names one: "that you believe in the one that he sent" (John 6:29). John 6 links believing with coming, seeing, hearing and eating: the one who believes "has eternal life" (John 6:47), the same promise later given to the one who eats and drinks (John 6:54).

sections.h: Equal in honor, receiving all from the Father (John 5)
sections.b: John 5:17–30 was a key passage in the debates that led to the doctrine of the Trinity. The Son does what the Father does, gives life and judges, and is to be honored as the Father is honored (John 5:21–23), yet he can do nothing on his own and has life because the Father gave it to him (John 5:19, 26). Nicene writers such as Athanasius and Augustine read this as eternal sonship, equal and yet from the Father; Arians read it as proof that the Son is lesser; Unitarians and Jehovah's Witnesses read "equal to God" (John 5:18) as only the opponents' charge.

sections.h: John 5–6 and the later charge against "the Jews"
sections.b: In John 5 "the Jews" seek to kill Jesus for healing on the Sabbath and calling God his own Father (John 5:16–18), and Jesus tells them that Moses will accuse them (John 5:45). Later Christian writers lifted such lines out of their setting, an argument among Jews about the Sabbath and the reading of Moses, and used them to blame the Jewish people as a whole. Jewish scholars such as Adele Reinhartz ask readers to see who is meant in each scene (the Temple authorities in John 5, a Galilean crowd in John 6) and to read John's harsh words as part of a painful split between church and synagogue.

sections.h: Signs at the pool, on the hills and on the sea (John 5–6)
sections.b: John calls Jesus's miracles "signs" because they point to who he is. In John 5 a word heals a man ill for thirty-eight years, and the healing on a Sabbath leads to the claim that the Son does the Father's work (John 5:17). In John 6 the feeding of five thousand, the only miracle in all four Gospels, leads to "I am the bread of life" (John 6:35), and the walk on the sea shows Jesus doing what Scripture says only God does (Job 9:8). Yet John also shows that signs do not force faith: the crowd wants more bread, and the healed man reports Jesus to the authorities.
